**Fashion Weeks**  
Paris is synonymous with style, and fashionistas will be in seventh heaven during the city’s haute couture fashion weeks, held each year in January and June/July. If freedom and fireworks are your thing, what better time to be in Paris than 14 July, or Bastille Day, when the city celebrates the storming of the hated prison that became a symbol of repression and aristocratic excess. Watch the military parade down the Champs-Élysées, enjoy the Eiffel Tower fireworks from the Champ de Mars, and raise a glass to *liberté, égalité* and *fraternité*. No guillotines allowed—and with most of the metros closed, be prepared to walk home.

**Paris Plages**  
It is still true that many Paris residents leave the city in August, shutting up shop and heading to the beach. Yet for the past few years, Paris Plages has brought that holiday spirit into the city itself. Sand dunes, swimming pools, and pétanque may be things you associate with France’s south coast resorts, but all can be found along the riverbank from late July until late August each year.

**The FIAC (International Fair of Contemporary Art)**  
October’s *Foire Internationale d’Art Contemporain* (FIAC) sees gallery owners and collectors of contemporary art descend on the Louvre and the Grand Palais for one of the art world’s major events. The fair places an emphasis on up-and-coming artists and newer galleries from across Europe. Works in every medium—painting, drawing, prints, photography, sculpture, and more—are on display and available to purchase.

**Ice Skating in Front of the Hôtel de Ville**  
If you like your outdoor pursuits frosty and free, you’ll love the ice rink outside the Hôtel de Ville, open every year from December until March. Rent skates or bring your own and glide around the rink, hand in hand with a loved one, gazing at the beautiful buildings that surround the square. counterfactuals.output:
# Paris by Season: The Best Annual Events and Experiences in the City of Light

Paris is never just one city. In spring, it’s a runway. In summer, it becomes a riverside resort. By autumn, the art world moves in. And in winter, even the city’s grand plazas can feel like scenes from a snow globe.

For travelers, timing a visit around one of Paris’ signature annual events can turn a classic trip — museums, cafés, monuments, late-night walks along the Seine — into something more atmospheric. From the spectacle of Fashion Week to the fireworks of Bastille Day, here are some of the best seasonal events and activities to experience in the French capital.

## Spring and Fall: Paris Fashion Week

Few events capture Paris’ global influence quite like Fashion Week. Held several times a year, with major women’s ready-to-wear shows typically in late winter/early spring and early fall, Paris Fashion Week brings designers, models, editors, celebrities and street-style photographers to the city.

Most runway shows are industry-only, but visitors can still feel the energy. The areas around the Louvre, Palais de Tokyo, Grand Palais, Place Vendôme and the Marais often become impromptu stages, with photographers gathering outside venues and sharply dressed attendees sweeping between shows.

Even without an invitation, travelers can lean into the moment: browse the boutiques of Rue Saint-Honoré, explore the concept stores of Le Marais, visit fashion exhibitions at the Palais Galliera or Musée des Arts Décoratifs, or book a table at a people-watching café near the fashion circuit.

**Best for:** Design lovers, luxury shoppers, street-style fans  
**When to go:** February/March and September/October for major women’s collections

## July: Bastille Day

France’s national holiday, celebrated on July 14, is one of the most memorable days to be in Paris. Known in France as *La Fête Nationale*, Bastille Day marks the storming of the Bastille in 1789 and the beginning of the French Revolution.

The day begins with a grand military parade along the Champs-Élysées, attended by French officials and watched by crowds lining the avenue. Aircraft fly overhead trailing the blue, white and red of the French flag, while cavalry, military bands and ceremonial units move toward Place de la Concorde.

By evening, attention shifts to the Eiffel Tower. The Bastille Day fireworks show, launched from the tower and the Trocadéro gardens, is one of Europe’s most dramatic urban displays. Many Parisians and visitors gather on the Champ de Mars, along the Seine or at elevated viewpoints across the city.

The night before or around the holiday, fire stations across Paris often host traditional *bals des pompiers* — lively firefighters’ balls with music, dancing and a neighborhood party atmosphere.

**Best for:** First-time visitors, families, photographers, night owls  
**When to go:** July 13-14  
**Tip:** Arrive early for fireworks viewing spots, and expect major crowds and security checkpoints.

## Summer: Paris Plages

Paris may be hundreds of miles from the Mediterranean, but each summer the city brings the beach to the Seine.

Paris Plages, usually held from July into late August or early September, transforms stretches of the riverbanks and canal areas into summer leisure zones. Expect deck chairs, parasols, misting stations, pop-up activities, games, concerts and family-friendly programming. In some years, swimming areas and water activities are also offered at the Bassin de la Villette.

What makes Paris Plages so appealing is its relaxed, local feel. It’s not about sightseeing in the traditional sense; it’s about slowing down. After a morning at the Louvre or Notre-Dame area, travelers can settle into a lounge chair, buy an ice cream, watch boats pass and experience a version of Paris that feels more neighborhood than postcard.

**Best for:** Families, budget travelers, summer visitors, anyone needing a break from museums  
**When to go:** July to late August/early September  
**Tip:** Visit on a weekday morning or early evening for a calmer atmosphere.

## Autumn: FIAC and Paris’ Contemporary Art Season

For decades, FIAC — the Foire Internationale d’Art Contemporain — was one of Paris’ premier contemporary art fairs, drawing collectors, galleries, curators and artists from around the world. Traditionally held in October, it helped anchor Paris’ fall art calendar and brought major international galleries into conversation with the city’s museums and historic spaces.

While the Paris art fair landscape has evolved in recent years, autumn remains one of the strongest seasons for contemporary art in the capital. Major fairs, gallery openings, museum exhibitions and off-site installations often cluster around October, creating a citywide cultural moment.

Visitors can pair fair-related events with stops at the Centre Pompidou, Palais de Tokyo, Fondation Louis Vuitton, Bourse de Commerce – Pinault Collection and the galleries of the Marais and Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Even for casual art lovers, fall in Paris offers the feeling that something new is opening every night.

**Best for:** Art collectors, museumgoers, culture-focused travelers  
**When to go:** October  
**Tip:** Check current fair schedules before booking, as names, venues and formats can change from year to year.

## Winter: Ice Skating at Hôtel de Ville

Winter gives Paris a different kind of magic. The plane trees are bare, café terraces glow under heaters and holiday lights brighten the grand boulevards. One of the city’s most beloved seasonal traditions has been ice skating at the Hôtel de Ville, the ornate city hall in the heart of Paris.

When the rink is installed, the square in front of Hôtel de Ville becomes a festive gathering place, with skaters gliding beneath the neo-Renaissance façade. It’s especially atmospheric after dark, when the building is illuminated and the surrounding streets lead toward the Seine, Notre-Dame and the Marais.

Seasonal ice rinks in Paris can vary by year and location, so travelers should confirm current winter offerings before planning around a specific rink. But whether at Hôtel de Ville or another festive venue, skating in Paris is a charming way to break up museum days and winter shopping.

**Best for:** Couples, families, holiday travelers  
**When to go:** December to early March, depending on the year  
**Tip:** Bring gloves, check whether skate rental is available and consider going on a weekday to avoid long lines.

## More Seasonal Reasons to Visit Paris

Beyond the headline events, Paris’ calendar is packed with seasonal pleasures.

In spring, cherry blossoms and magnolias bloom in parks like Jardin des Plantes, Parc de Sceaux and Square Jean XXIII near Notre-Dame. Café terraces fill up again, and the city feels freshly awake.

In early summer, the Fête de la Musique on June 21 turns streets, squares and bars into free concert venues. Later in the season, open-air cinema and outdoor festivals pop up around the city.

In autumn, the grape harvest festival in Montmartre, known as the Fête des Vendanges, celebrates the neighborhood’s small vineyard with parades, tastings and music. The changing leaves in the Luxembourg Gardens and Père Lachaise Cemetery make fall one of the most photogenic times to wander.

In winter, Christmas markets, department store window displays and holiday lights along the Champs-Élysées bring a festive glow, while January offers quieter museums and post-holiday sales.

## When Is the Best Time to Visit Paris?

There is no wrong season to visit Paris — only a different version of the city waiting to be discovered.

For spectacle, July brings Bastille Day and Paris Plages. For style, plan around Fashion Week. For culture, October is a standout month thanks to the contemporary art calendar associated with FIAC and its successors. For romance and atmosphere, winter offers lights, skating and fewer crowds.

The best strategy may be to choose the event that matches your interests, then leave enough unscheduled time to do what Paris does best: surprise you. A fashion week street scene, a riverside beach chair, a burst of fireworks over the Eiffel Tower or a turn around a winter ice rink can become the memory that defines the trip.

## Paris: When to Visit, Month by Month

Paris is a year-round destination, but the best time to go depends on what kind of magic you’re after—spring blossoms, summer festivals, fashion buzz, or cozy winter lights.

### January–February: Quiet Museums & Winter Sales  
Paris starts the year crisp, calm, and atmospheric. It’s a great time for crowd-free visits to the Louvre, Musée d’Orsay, and Versailles. January also brings **les soldes**, the official winter sales, making it ideal for shopping.  
**Travel notes:** Pack warm layers and waterproof shoes. Hotel prices are often lower, but days are short.

### March–April: Spring Blooms & Easter Breaks  
As café terraces reawaken and cherry blossoms appear in parks like **Jardin des Plantes** and **Parc de Sceaux**, Paris feels fresh and romantic. Easter holidays can bring more families and higher prices.  
**Travel notes:** Weather is changeable—bring a light coat and umbrella. Book popular restaurants ahead.

### May–June: Festivals, Long Days & Outdoor Paris  
This is one of the loveliest times to visit. Expect long evenings, picnics along the Seine, and major events like the **French Open at Roland-Garros** and **Fête de la Musique** on June 21, when live music spills into streets and squares.  
**Travel notes:** This is peak season for good reason. Reserve hotels early and expect busy attractions.

### July–August: Summer Buzz & Bastille Day  
July brings fireworks, parades, and patriotic celebration for **Bastille Day** on July 14. The city also hosts **Paris Plages**, when parts of the Seine are transformed into urban “beaches.” August is quieter in local neighborhoods as many Parisians leave on holiday.  
**Travel notes:** Some small restaurants and shops close in August. Major sights stay open, but book tickets in advance.

### September–October: Fashion, Wine & Golden Light  
September is stylish and energetic, with **Paris Fashion Week** drawing designers, celebrities, and photographers. October brings autumn colors, cultural exhibitions, and the lively **Montmartre Grape Harvest Festival**.  
**Travel notes:** September is still busy and pricey. October is cooler and often excellent for walking.

### November–December: Cozy Cafés & Christmas Sparkle  
Late autumn is moody and beautiful, perfect for lingering in bistros and bookstores. By December, Paris glows with festive lights, department store windows, and Christmas markets at spots like the Tuileries.  
**Travel notes:** Bring a warm coat and plan for rain. December weekends can be busy around shopping districts.

## Best Overall Time to Visit  
For pleasant weather, lively events, and classic Paris charm, visit in **May, June, September, or October**. For lower prices and fewer crowds, choose **January, February, or November**.

# PARIS, France (CNN)

Paris is never content to be merely beautiful. Across the calendar, the French capital transforms itself again and again — into a runway, a riverside resort, an open-air theater, an art-world crossroads and, in winter, a city of sparkling ice.

For travelers, that means there is no single “best” time to visit Paris. There is only the question of which Paris you want to meet.

In January and July, the city’s most glamorous face comes into focus during haute couture fashion week, when historic maisons and emerging designers unveil hand-crafted collections to an audience of editors, celebrities, buyers and devoted style-watchers. While most runway shows are invitation-only, the atmosphere spills into the streets: outside grand venues, photographers gather, impeccably dressed guests sweep past, and cafés in the fashion districts hum with speculation about silhouettes, fabrics and the next headline-making look.

Summer brings a different spectacle. On July 14, Bastille Day — France’s national holiday — Paris stages one of Europe’s most memorable celebrations. The day begins with military pageantry on the Champs-Élysées and builds toward nightfall, when crowds gather around the Champ de Mars, bridges and riverbanks for fireworks over the Eiffel Tower. Set against the city’s most famous landmark, the display is both patriotic and cinematic, a burst of color above one of the world’s most recognizable skylines.

By then, another seasonal ritual is underway: Paris Plages. Each summer, stretches of the Seine and canal-side areas are reimagined as urban beaches, with deck chairs, parasols, pop-up cafés, misting stations, games and cultural events. It is Paris at its most playful — less about monuments and more about lingering. Families picnic, office workers pause for a lunch-hour escape, and visitors discover that the city can do leisure with as much flair as it does history.

In autumn, Paris turns its attention indoors — though the energy remains thoroughly international. The city’s contemporary art fair draws galleries, collectors, curators and artists from around the world, reinforcing Paris’ renewed status as a major art-market capital. Beyond the fair itself, satellite exhibitions, museum openings and gallery shows animate neighborhoods from the Marais to Saint-Germain-des-Prés. For travelers, it is an ideal moment to pair the blockbuster institutions — the Louvre, Musée d’Orsay and Centre Pompidou — with smaller galleries and experimental spaces.

Then winter arrives, and Paris becomes intimate. Holiday lights line the boulevards, department-store windows become miniature stages, and outdoor ice rinks appear in atmospheric settings across the city. Skating beneath festive illuminations or near historic architecture offers a seasonal pleasure that feels both local and romantic. Afterward, there is always hot chocolate, onion soup or a glass of red wine waiting in a nearby café.

What connects these events is not simply spectacle, but the Parisian talent for turning public life into performance. Fashion week makes the sidewalk a stage. Bastille Day turns the skyline into theater. Paris Plages converts the riverbanks into a shared summer living room. The art fair transforms the city into a global conversation. Ice skating adds movement and laughter to winter’s long evenings.

For repeat visitors, these signature events offer a reason to see familiar landmarks in a new light. For first-timers, they provide a vivid introduction to a city that is constantly balancing grandeur with reinvention.

Paris may be timeless, but it is never still.

# Paris, Season by Season: The Best Special Things to Do Throughout the Year

Paris is never exactly out of season. In winter, the city glows under café awnings and museum lights. In spring, its gardens seem to exhale all at once. Summer brings long evenings along the Seine, while autumn turns the boulevards cinematic and the cultural calendar roars back to life.

For travelers, the trick is not simply deciding whether to visit Paris, but when — because each season offers a different version of the city. Here are some of the most memorable things to do in Paris at different times of year.

## Winter: Lights, Markets and Museum-Hopping

Paris in winter can be brisk, gray and occasionally wet — but it is also one of the most atmospheric times to visit. The crowds are thinner than in peak months, hotel rates can be more forgiving, and the city’s indoor treasures come into their own.

In December, Christmas lights transform major avenues and elegant shopping streets. The Champs-Élysées, Avenue Montaigne and Place Vendôme are known for their polished displays, while department stores such as Galeries Lafayette and Printemps unveil elaborate holiday windows that draw families, photographers and curious passersby.

Seasonal markets pop up across the city, offering mulled wine, roasted chestnuts, crafts and winter snacks. For a classic holiday outing, combine a market visit with a spin on an ice rink if one is operating that season, or simply wander through illuminated neighborhoods as dusk falls early.

Winter is also prime museum season. The Louvre, Musée d’Orsay, Centre Pompidou and Musée de l’Orangerie are obvious choices, but colder days are ideal for smaller gems too: the Musée Rodin, Musée Carnavalet, Musée Jacquemart-André or the Musée de la Vie Romantique. A long lunch afterward — onion soup, steak frites, a glass of red wine — feels less like a break from sightseeing and more like part of the Paris winter ritual.

## Spring: Blossoms, Gardens and Café Terraces

Spring may be the season most closely associated with Paris for good reason. By March and April, the city begins to bloom, and Parisians reclaim terraces, parks and riverbanks with visible relief.

One of the loveliest spring pleasures is searching for blossoms. Cherry trees flower in pockets around the city, including parts of the Jardin des Plantes, Parc de Sceaux just outside Paris, and certain corners near the Eiffel Tower and Notre-Dame. Magnolias, wisteria and tulips follow in gardens and courtyards, adding flashes of color to the city’s limestone backdrop.

The Luxembourg Gardens are especially appealing in spring, with chairs drawn around fountains and flowerbeds. The Tuileries, Parc Monceau and the elevated Coulée Verte René-Dumont — a leafy walkway built on a former railway line — also make fine seasonal strolls.

Spring is also a strong time for food lovers. Market stalls fill with asparagus, strawberries and early produce. Visiting an open-air market, such as Marché Bastille or Marché d’Aligre, offers a glimpse of everyday Paris at its most vibrant. Pick up cheese, bread and fruit for a picnic along the Seine or in one of the city’s parks.

By May, evening apéritifs spill onto sidewalks, and the city begins to feel almost Mediterranean in spirit. It is an ideal time to linger rather than rush.

## Summer: Seine-Side Evenings and Open-Air Culture

Summer in Paris is lively, social and increasingly outdoors. While July and August can bring heat — and some smaller restaurants and shops close for holidays in August — the city compensates with festivals, late sunsets and a relaxed rhythm.

The Seine becomes one of the main stages of Parisian life. Walk the riverbanks at golden hour, browse the bouquinistes’ green bookstalls, or settle on the stone quays with a picnic as boats glide past. Paris Plages, the city’s summer beach-style event, typically brings deckchairs, activities and a holiday mood to stretches of the river and canal areas.

Open-air cinema, concerts and cultural events often appear across the city in summer. The Parc de la Villette has hosted outdoor film screenings, while music and dance events animate parks, squares and courtyards. June’s Fête de la Musique, when musicians perform across Paris in streets, bars and public spaces, is one of the city’s great free celebrations.

Summer is also a good time to explore Paris by neighborhood. Canal Saint-Martin and the Bassin de la Villette are popular for waterside drinks and casual dining. Montmartre is best tackled early in the morning before the crowds climb toward Sacré-Cœur. In the Marais, long evenings are suited to gallery visits, boutique browsing and dinner that stretches late.

For a classic excursion, take a day trip to Versailles, where the gardens are in full seasonal splendor. Fountain shows and musical garden events often run during the warmer months, adding grandeur to an already extravagant visit.

## Autumn: Art, Wine and Golden Streets

Autumn may be Paris’s most underrated season. The summer crowds fade, the air sharpens, and the city returns to its full working rhythm. Cultural life intensifies, with new exhibitions, theater seasons, fashion events and gallery openings filling the calendar.

This is a particularly good time for art-minded travelers. Major museums often launch significant exhibitions in the fall, and contemporary art spaces across the city become busier after the quieter summer period. The Grand Palais, when programming is active, the Fondation Louis Vuitton, Palais de Tokyo and smaller galleries in the Marais and Belleville all reward attention.

Autumn also brings one of Paris’s most charming local traditions: the Montmartre Grape Harvest Festival, or Fête des Vendanges de Montmartre. Held in October, it celebrates the small vineyard on the hill with parades, tastings, concerts and neighborhood festivities. It is crowded, yes, but it offers a rare village-like atmosphere in the middle of the capital.

For seasonal beauty, walk through Père Lachaise Cemetery, Parc des Buttes-Chaumont or the Luxembourg Gardens as leaves turn gold and copper. The city’s cafés also regain their cozy appeal. This is the season for hot chocolate at a grand salon, a long bistro dinner or a rainy afternoon spent reading under a covered terrace.

Autumn is also excellent for culinary wandering. Markets fill with mushrooms, pears, apples, squash and game. Wine bars feel especially inviting, and the city’s bistros lean into richer dishes as temperatures cool.

## When Paris Feels Most Local

Beyond the four seasons, some of the best times to visit Paris are shaped by the city’s calendar rather than the weather.

In January and June, the government-regulated sales periods, known as *les soldes*, bring discounts to department stores, boutiques and designer shops. Fashion lovers can make a serious sport of bargain hunting.

In February, Valentine’s Day may draw couples, but the more interesting romantic gesture is simply choosing an old-fashioned Paris evening: a neighborhood restaurant, a moonlit bridge and perhaps a nightcap in a hotel bar.

In July, Bastille Day on July 14 brings a military parade on the Champs-Élysées and fireworks near the Eiffel Tower. It is one of the busiest but most spectacular nights of the year.

In September, European Heritage Days often open normally closed government buildings, private mansions and historic sites to the public. It is a remarkable opportunity for architecture and history enthusiasts.

## The Best Time to Go? It Depends on the Paris You Want

First-time visitors often gravitate toward spring and early autumn, when the weather is pleasant and the city looks effortlessly beautiful. Summer suits travelers who want festivals, river evenings and a more open-air version of Paris. Winter favors museum lovers, shoppers and anyone drawn to a quieter, moodier city.

But Paris has a way of making each season feel like the right one. The same street can be festive under December lights, fragrant with blossoms in April, sunlit at 10 p.m. in June and carpeted with leaves in October.

That is the enduring appeal of the French capital: it does not offer just one Paris, but many. The best visit may be the one that matches the season — and then leaves you wanting to come back for the next.

## Paris Through the Seasons: Iconic Events Worth Planning Around

Paris is always a good idea—but the city changes personality beautifully with the calendar. From couture-filled winter weeks to summer celebrations on the Seine and atmospheric holiday skating, here are some of the most iconic seasonal attractions to experience in the French capital.

### January: Fashion Takes Center Stage

Paris begins the year in high style. January brings major fashion events, including men’s fashion week and haute couture presentations, when the city becomes a stage for designers, editors, models, and street-style photographers. Even if you don’t have a front-row invitation, the energy spills into neighborhoods like the 1st, 8th, and Marais, where luxury boutiques, palace hotels, and café terraces become part of the spectacle.

For visitors, it’s a glamorous time to explore the city’s fashion heritage: the Palais Galliera fashion museum, designer flagships along Avenue Montaigne, and the elegant department stores of Boulevard Haussmann. Winter sales also make January a prime month for shopping.

### Spring: Gardens, Terraces, and Museum Days

As the weather softens, Paris moves outdoors. Cherry blossoms and fresh greenery brighten the Jardin des Plantes, Parc Monceau, and the Tuileries, while café terraces refill with locals lingering over espresso. Spring is also an excellent season for cultural sightseeing, with fewer crowds than peak summer and a full calendar of exhibitions.

Classic stops—the Louvre, Musée d’Orsay, Centre Pompidou, and Musée de l’Orangerie—feel especially rewarding before the high-season rush. A spring walk along the Seine, past booksellers and bridges, offers the kind of Paris scene visitors imagine long before they arrive.

### July: Bastille Day and Summer on the Seine

July delivers one of Paris’s grandest moments: Bastille Day on July 14. The national holiday begins with a military parade along the Champs-Élysées and ends with fireworks near the Eiffel Tower, a spectacular display that draws crowds to the Champ de Mars, Trocadéro, and riverbanks.

Summer also transforms the Seine into a public playground. Paris Plages, the city’s seasonal “beaches,” bring lounge chairs, umbrellas, pop-up activities, and a festive waterfront atmosphere to the riverbanks and canals. It’s less about swimming and more about slowing down—reading by the water, joining an open-air activity, or watching golden-hour light fall across the bridges.

### Late Summer: Open-Air Paris

As temperatures rise, Paris leans into al fresco living. Outdoor cinemas, concerts, night markets, and rooftop bars help define the season. Neighborhoods like Canal Saint-Martin and the Bassin de la Villette are especially lively, while evening river cruises offer breezy views of illuminated landmarks.

This is also a good time to discover a different rhythm of the city: picnic in the Luxembourg Gardens, explore the village-like streets of Montmartre early in the morning, or follow the Seine by bike as the city slows into long summer evenings.

### October: Art Fairs and Cultural Energy

Autumn brings a sophisticated buzz to Paris, particularly in October, when the city’s art scene takes the spotlight. International art fairs, gallery openings, and museum events attract collectors, curators, and culture-minded travelers from around the world.

The Grand Palais area, the Marais, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and contemporary galleries across the city become key stops during this art-filled period. Even beyond the fairs, October is one of the best months to visit: the weather is crisp, the crowds are lighter, and the city’s parks turn shades of gold.

### Winter: Lights, Markets, and Skating

By winter, Paris glows. Holiday lights decorate major avenues and department store windows become elaborate seasonal displays, particularly at Galeries Lafayette and Printemps. Christmas markets appear around the city, offering mulled wine, sweets, crafts, and festive snacks.

Ice skating has become one of the city’s favorite winter traditions, with seasonal rinks often appearing in landmark settings depending on the year. Whether beneath a glass-roofed venue, near a historic square, or beside a festive village, skating in Paris adds a playful note to the colder months.

### The Takeaway

Paris is not a one-season city. January brings fashion glamour, July delivers national celebration and riverside summer life, October highlights the global art scene, and winter wraps the capital in lights and holiday charm. Whenever you visit, the city offers a different version of itself—always recognizable, always cinematic, and always worth another trip.
